principle: Make every call for the player, not for the developers' convenience
why: Players don't care why developers did something; they only care whether the game is good, and they won't cut you slack because development was hard. Every developer shares one goal, entertaining players, and that same goal is what keeps you motivated through a hard project.
how_to_apply: When a spec or compromise exists to make development easier, ask whether players would accept it; keep it only if it is a sensible efficiency trade they won't notice, otherwise look for alternatives together with the programmers. When you feel lost or unmotivated, ask how the decision in front of you entertains the player and let that decide. Remember that real people will buy what you make.
anti_pattern: Design documents that put the developers' jobs ahead of the player experience; expecting players to forgive problems because development was difficult.
example: Sakurai's answer to design documents that prioritize developer convenience (ep 21); his rule for when you've lost your way: entertain players (ep 7); remembering that actual people will buy the game (ep 67).
review_question: Which decisions in this build were made for our convenience, and would a player accept each one?
keywords: player first player perspective player experience developer convenience compromise entertain players purpose motivation customer

principle: Treat each project as a professional assignment, not a hobby
why: Once money, sales and numbers are involved, game development is a job like any other; indie developers become professionals too, and being a pro means responding to demand. Once you understand what makes games fun, you can make any kind of experience regardless of your own taste. Sakurai says he makes games because it is what he is best at and suited for, not because they are the games he wants to play.
how_to_apply: At kickoff, write down the genre, goal and audience the project must serve and design to that brief. On tasks that aren't to your taste, find what makes them interesting and do them well anyway. Give a sequel the same full effort as an original, and practice working in styles outside your specialty so you can match a set style.
anti_pattern: Designing games for yourself; only putting effort into work you personally enjoy; coasting on a series' name.
example: An experienced gamer making Kirby's Dream Land for newcomers, and Meteos despite not being good at block puzzles; an artist who loves cute things texturing lifelike zombies and roaches; artists on one team matching a single visual style.
review_question: Can you state the genre, goal and audience this game must serve, and does the build serve them rather than your own taste?
keywords: professionalism professional assignment brief job not a hobby personal taste career genre audience sequel range

principle: Refuse easy-way-out compromises: the hardship fades, the game endures
why: You forget the difficulty of a project but never the parts you got wrong, because flaws stay in the game for good. Every player multiplies your effort: if 1,000 people play, the impact is 1,000 times your hardship. Most creative works also have to do something extra to stand out from the crowd.
how_to_apply: Before taking a shortcut, ask whether you'll regret it once the game ships. Set up an efficient workflow first, then put the effort you save into what players will actually experience. Decide which special touches will set the game apart and commit to them.
anti_pattern: Taking the easy way out with too many compromises. Equally, needless hardship: Sakurai is explicit that effort should serve customers, not be suffering for its own sake.
example: The ending of Kirby's Adventure, where the screen shakes when it was supposed to flash white, a slip he still remembers; Melee's orchestral arrangements and first CG movie, whose storyboards he drew over his New Year's holiday; Smash Ultimate's 29 million-plus sales, about the population of Australia.
review_question: Which compromise in this build will you still regret when the game has been out for years?
keywords: polish compromise shortcut regret quality bar extra effort stand out hardship impact multiplied efficiency

principle: Start now: motivation arrives after your hands are moving
why: Turning a 0 into a 1 is hard, and overthinking while unmotivated goes nowhere; motivation comes later, once you've started. The best way to improve is steady output, and the words you tell yourself set the course of your actions: those who act are the ones who win.
how_to_apply: Take the first physical step at once: open the document and type a line, open the canvas and draw. Cut off social media, video sites and games before a work block. Psych yourself up out loud and start. Save planning tricks such as visualizing tasks for after you've begun. If you want to make games, sit down and make one with whatever tool you have.
anti_pattern: Waiting to feel motivated; overthinking what the work means before doing it; waiting for better tools.
example: His exaggerated advice to work as if a bomb in the room will go off unless you start now (ep 83); 'Do it! Come on! Go!' (ep 212); Family BASIC, bought with six months of allowance, is what showed him he could make games (ep 118).
review_question: What is the very first physical action on this task, and why haven't you taken it yet?
keywords: motivation procrastination getting started just do it action momentum productivity distractions focus

principle: Manufacture urgency, and favor speed over endlessly polishing drafts
why: Thinking you can finish whenever lets work drift, while telling yourself only a few hours remain gets things done. Momentum counts for a lot: the longer a proposal sits, the less fresh it gets. With limited time, over-working every line to prevent misunderstanding costs succinctness.
how_to_apply: Give each task a short self-imposed time limit, set well ahead of the real deadline, and frame milestones as something closing in on you. Once the outline and main points are itemized, write the whole draft in one push. Accept small imperfections in proposals, scripts and presentations and live with the results.
anti_pattern: Treating work as something you can finish whenever; leaving it to the real last day like summer homework; ruminating over every detail of a draft.
example: He went from last to first in a middle-school race by imagining a three-meter machine chasing him (ep 171); he wrote the channel's scripts in about a month, roughly 12 a day: 'Short and snappy! Speed above all else!' (ep 261).
review_question: Does this task have a near, self-imposed deadline, and is any draft stalling because you keep polishing it?
keywords: deadline urgency speed momentum time limit power of suggestion hot and fast perfectionism drafts pace

principle: Take a lot in: play many current games to the end, reflectively
why: A director needs to grasp the scope of modern games so that what they deliver is on par; Sakurai calls this a must. Input you don't reflect on goes in one ear and out the other. Fun is relative to its time, so judging everything by the games of your youth blinds you to the present.
how_to_apply: Play as many different current games as you can rather than one title at length, and try to reach each ending. While playing or watching, note what works and why. Choose the input form that suits you (film works too if you reflect on it). Before claiming old games were better, replay one next to a recent game.
anti_pattern: Sinking all your play time into one game; passive consumption; holding modern games to nostalgic standards.
example: Sakurai keeps playing many games even when busy and always tries to see the ending (ep 126); he tells fans who have put thousands of hours into his competitive games to be sure to play other games too (ep 220).
review_question: How many recent games in or near your genre have you finished this year, and what did you write down about each?
keywords: input research playing games broad input reflect study competitors modern games nostalgia references media diet

principle: Put a lot out: keep a small, steady, low-pressure output habit
why: You won't succeed without steady output, and regular writing is training. A habit survives for years when each installment costs little time, uses strengths you already exercise, and isn't done out of obligation; working out of duty or for the sake of the industry takes a major toll. Habits compound: his column habit is what led to the channel.
how_to_apply: Commit to a recurring output such as a devlog, column, daily team report or daily screenshot. Time-box each installment to a short fixed slot. Publish what you think is good instead of writing for an imagined audience. Before starting a side project, fix its total run and the size of each edition so it fits beside your main work.
anti_pattern: Taking on routine work out of obligation; overthinking each installment; open-ended side projects that grow until they compete with development.
example: His Weekly Famitsu column ran 18 years and 9 months, 640 articles, usually written in about an hour (ep 98); a Daily Report every workday and the Screenshot of the Day (ep 123, 126); PRESS START planned from the start as a 10-year run of 14 to 16 pieces per concert (ep 116).
review_question: What do you produce on a fixed rhythm, and is each installment small enough to survive your busiest month?
keywords: output habit routine devlog column daily report consistency sustainable time-box obligation side project writing

principle: Clear every review the same day, and protect a block for your own work
why: Every review that waits keeps teammates waiting, and delaying a key member's decision can put a whole team behind; quick replies also make the second and third rounds easier, and putting things off just makes the next day worse. But being open to reviews all day breaks a lead's schedule into erratic pieces.
how_to_apply: Take review requests through one channel with a fixed subject line and handle them first come, first served. Reply the same day, ideally as soon as the current review is done, and explain any changes to everyone involved. Set a delivery cutoff so reviews never start late at night, and reserve a fixed period (mornings, or after a cutoff) with no reviews at all for your own tasks.
anti_pattern: Letting requests pile up overnight; leaving yourself open to supervision all day; reviews arriving so late they wreck your sleep.
example: Sakurai's email-only 'Review Request' workflow, answered within the day no matter how many pile up (ep 177); his channel editors had to deliver by 8 PM after 11 PM deliveries left him short of sleep (ep 261).
review_question: How many review requests or decisions are more than a day old, and when is your protected no-review block?
keywords: reviews same day turnaround supervision inbox email decision speed cutoff time blocking productivity bottleneck habits

principle: Define the problem's theme, then list many ideas before pruning
why: If you try to think of something from nothing you have no starting point, so ideas naturally won't come. Producing many candidates, even silly or unrealistic ones, gets you past the feeling of having nothing, and minor variants of failed ideas often lead to the answer. Sakurai treats improving games and coming up with new ideas as learnable skills.
how_to_apply: Write the problem as a simple one-line theme. List broad solution types and note why each fails in this context. For every failure, look for a variant that fixes its flaw. Keep thinking actively instead of waiting for inspiration, and prune only once the list is long.
anti_pattern: Brainstorming with no defined problem; throwing out minor or silly ideas too early.
example: 'How to put out a fire in some ruins': no water nearby; sand is scarce but dirt might work; a bucket is too small but a bigger one might do (ep 237).
review_question: Can you state in one line the problem you're solving, and how many candidate solutions have you written down?
keywords: ideation ideas brainstorming problem solving creativity stuck creative block theme quantity over quality

principle: Ask why other games work, then rebuild instead of mimicking
why: Copying something fun won't make your game feel original; reexamining why other games do things raises your chances of making something fresh. If your game is too close to another, players can just play the original, and to stand out you need something that can't be found elsewhere.
how_to_apply: Before borrowing a mechanic, write down why it works in its source and whether that reason applies to your game. Deconstruct the fun into its parts (usually risk and reward), analyze it, and rebuild it as your own mechanic. If you start from an homage, list many reasons a player would pick yours over the original, not just one.
anti_pattern: Mimicking features without understanding them; riding an original's coattails with a single point of difference.
example: Kirby Air Ride's charge-and-release drifting came from deconstructing why drifting is fun, not from imitating racing games (ep 57).
review_question: For each borrowed mechanic, can you say why it works in its source and what makes your version yours?
keywords: originality copying imitation homage deconstruct analyze rebuild innovation fresh mimic why

principle: Train a keen personal eye, and put your own take into the game
why: The one thing the skilled directors Sakurai knows share is a sensibility that latches onto tiny details and perceives what others miss, in visuals, game essence, animation and story. Directors use their own thoughts and feelings to set their games apart; the role, like a game, calls for a touch only that person can offer. That quirkiness still needs balance and the ability to communicate it.
how_to_apply: When reviewing your build or someone else's game, write down the small details most people would overlook and what you would change. For each major decision, state your personal take and how it differs from the genre's usual answer, and keep the difference on purpose. Practice explaining the idea until teammates can repeat it back.
anti_pattern: Assuming there is one standard way to direct and copying it; idiosyncrasy you can't communicate to a team.
example: In supervision he flags tiny flaws, such as an extraneous mark on a face or hair poking into an eye highlight, as soon as he finds them (ep 253).
review_question: What in this game could only have come from you, and could your team explain it?
keywords: sensibility unique perspective director personal touch eye for detail originality vision taste quirky observation

principle: Notice echo chambers and seek opinions from outside your circle
why: A flood of agreement makes you feel right even though plenty of people disagree, and an insular world hides problems that need solving. It happens with design ideas and with reviews every day. If you can't stay objective, your game ends up unbalanced, whether you play it safer or push it further. Online opinions about what is strong or weak gain momentum and seem truer than they are.
how_to_apply: When an idea gets nothing but praise, ask people outside that circle what is wrong with it. Before acting on reviews or social reactions, check whether you are only seeing the voices that agree. Form your own verdict on a game before reading what others think. When online claims spread, check them against data and actual play.
anti_pattern: Letting in only the opinions that validate you.
example: Despite online talk of strong and weak fighters, Smash Ultimate's worldwide online data put every fighter's win rate between 47.18% and 51.43% (ep 218).
review_question: Who outside your usual circle has criticized this idea, and what did they say?
keywords: echo chamber criticism objectivity feedback bias social media reviews outside opinions validation community

principle: Keep your deliberate direction; don't let outside voices sand it off
why: Sometimes taking a game in your own 'unbalanced' direction is what feels best, and it beats being swayed by other people; a unique vision gives a game distinctive strength. Decisions made by majority converge on the safest, most mediocre ideas, and ideas opposed during planning often turn out fun once built.
how_to_apply: Sort feedback into team concerns you should adapt to and outside pressure that would only make the game more ordinary, and protect the deliberate quirks. Let the person who holds the big picture make creative calls instead of counting votes, and use polls only as input. Back the call with reasons and with everything the team knows.
anti_pattern: Being swayed until the game loses its identity; settling creative direction by headcount; the opposite failure, dictating with paper-thin reasoning.
example: Metal Gear Solid 3's wound-treatment system reportedly had only four supporters on the team at first, yet turned out fun (ep 158); Sakurai polls his team out of curiosity but keeps the final call, as with the Mii Fighter outfit's white socks (ep 158).
review_question: Which distinctive choices have been softened because of outside pressure, and did those changes fix real problems?
keywords: conviction vision unique direction majority vote mediocre criticism outside pressure identity distinctive

principle: Steer by your concept when fatigue and doubt set in
why: Development is long, and once fatigue sets in it is easy to wonder what is supposed to be fun. The concept is like a lighthouse: change course and you get lost, and scrapping work wastes months of artists' and programmers' effort and demoralizes the team. Fun is hard to see on paper, so teams often only grasp it once the game is playable.
how_to_apply: Write the concept as one clear statement before production and don't move forward until it's that clear. When doubting, check decisions against it, and amplify emergent fun only if it heads toward the concept. In proposals, commit to the ideal spec instead of hedging with alternatives, then course-correct with the team.
anti_pattern: Changing direction midway because the game isn't turning out as expected; leaving a Plan B in the proposal so someone else has to decide.
example: People have told Sakurai after a project shipped, 'Now I see what you were getting at' (ep 187).
review_question: Can you state the concept in one line, and does the change you're considering move toward it?
keywords: concept lighthouse direction staying the course doubt fatigue plan b commitment conviction staying true

principle: Treat a rejection as your job to show the appeal better
why: A proposal has to make the people who provide funding and talent think 'We should definitely do this', so showing the game's appeal is the presenter's responsibility. A game unlike anything before runs into preconceptions, and proactively searching for new ways to explain it pays off later. Poor results rarely trace to one person.
how_to_apply: When a pitch is rejected, rework how it demonstrates the fun instead of blaming the reviewers. Describe the game on its own terms rather than by comparison. If press or partners dismiss the game, explain it to players yourself. When something underperforms, review the whole chain instead of hunting for one culprit.
anti_pattern: Telling yourself the other party has no taste; pinning failure on a single person.
example: When magazines ignored his document explaining the first Smash Bros.' push and pull, he turned it into the Smash Bros. DOJO!! site himself (ep 143, 245).
review_question: If this pitch were rejected tomorrow, what would you change about how it shows the fun?
keywords: rejection pitch proposal criticism resilience communicate appeal blame preconceptions setback persuasion

principle: Never fight or badmouth coworkers: the industry is small
why: Developers move between teams constantly, so someone you wronged may join your next team years later, and directors do ask about former teammates. Treating people poorly gets you excluded, and dislike comes straight back to you. You are responsible for your workplace's atmosphere, and fixating on difficult people steals attention from supportive ones. Company work is mutual support on a path you chose.
how_to_apply: Raise problems directly as constructive feedback, ideally with a proposed fix. If a situation doesn't suit you, step back instead of escalating. Finish or hand off your work before leaving. Never speak ill of anyone. Follow a partner company's rules. Meet trouble with calm analysis, and treat directions to others as requests, not orders.
anti_pattern: Fighting, acting selfishly, leaving on bad terms, abandoning a project to jump to the next job, holding grudges, thinking of your job as forced on you.
example: Directors at other companies ask Sakurai about former team members who are interviewing with them (ep 249); Mr. Iwata stayed calm and offered analysis where most people would lose their temper (ep 259).
review_question: If every teammate on this project joined your next one, would you be glad?
keywords: conflict reputation coworkers small industry respect professionalism workplace atmosphere feedback cooperation career

principle: Break in by finishing your own game and letting originality show
why: Making a game yourself is the quickest, if not only, way into the industry: you see which problems arise and how to solve them, and even designers need to think like programmers. Many people want to make games, so an imitative idea won't help your case. Imitation is fine while learning, and finishing anything at all is a feat.
how_to_apply: Start small in whatever tool you can get and finish it. Get people to play it (friends, free online release, or a sale if you're confident), find out what they think, then improve it or carry the lessons forward. Send an original game with your applications even if you don't meet every listed requirement, and enter open proposal calls.
anti_pattern: Waiting for ideal tools; submitting an imitative showcase; not applying because you lack one listed requirement.
example: Family BASIC on the Famicom was how Sakurai learned he could make games (ep 118); before entering the industry he won Sega's Associate Planner Certificate No. 004 through a public proposal promotion (ep 149).
review_question: Is there a finished, original game you could hand to someone today?
keywords: career breaking in portfolio first game indie job application originality student junior finish your game

principle: Keep a new idea sealed until its first draft is written
why: Talking about an idea makes you feel fulfilled, which releases the internal pressure that gives a proposal its force. A design document written without sharing a word burns hotter than one compiled from a brainstorm. Posting ideas or progress on social media vents the same pressure.
how_to_apply: Whenever you want to tell someone about the idea, write it into the document instead. Hold back work-in-progress posts while it takes shape. Consult colleagues for weak points and new ideas only once the draft is finished. Picture how people will react to keep yourself going.
anti_pattern: Talking an unfinished proposal through; using a group brainstorm in place of your own draft; venting ideas on social media mid-creation.
example: His balloon and pressure-cooker metaphors for internal pressure (ep 144).
review_question: Did you finish a full first draft before pitching or posting about it?
keywords: internal pressure secrecy proposal draft brainstorming social media sharing ideas creative energy

principle: Turn negative thoughts into questions about how to improve
why: Each time you think, say or post a defeatist idea it becomes a little more true, because your thoughts and words set your attitude. Negative feelings are fine to have, and used as motivation they can be a bigger opportunity for change than a positive outlook.
how_to_apply: Stop voicing or posting defeatist lines about your work. Rewrite each one as a question and act on the answer: 'my work feels pointless' becomes 'what are some ways I can make it better?'
anti_pattern: Repeating negative ideas out loud or on social media; mistaking this for forced positivity that denies the feeling.
example: His examples of self-talk to avoid: 'I'm running out of money', 'There's barely any point in working', 'Life's just not fun' (ep 212).
review_question: What negative statement about this project have you repeated lately, and what improvement question does it hide?
keywords: mindset self-talk negativity motivation reframing attitude social media defeatism mental health

principle: Protect your body: exercise a little and fix your workstation
why: People who exercise tend to be far more productive than people who don't. Screens close to your eyes cause strain, and nothing works as well as changing the work environment; missing desks and chairs cause health problems. Overdoing it backfires.
how_to_apply: Do at least a little regular exercise, for example pedaling an exercise bike through play sessions. Keep about a meter between your eyes and the monitor (move it back if it is under 60 cm, and use a larger screen to compensate) and match brightness to the room. Make sure everyone has a proper desk and chair. Ramp up gradually and stop if something hurts.
anti_pattern: Overdoing it; long sessions with a screen close to your eyes; treating glasses or eyedrops as a substitute for fixing the setup.
example: Two-hour exercise-bike sessions, and legs hurt from climbing around 500 stairs (ep 24); severe eye strain during Smash Ultimate's development (ep 81); Sora buying desks and chairs for remote staff (ep 66).
review_question: Is your screen about a meter away, and when did you last exercise?
keywords: health exercise eye strain ergonomics monitor distance desk chair sleep burnout sustainable pace wellbeing

principle: Give one project all of you, and keep overhead off creative time
why: A project that needs its director's full time suffers when attention is split. Creators who go independent and hire staff often get bogged down in the management needed to keep employees paid, leaving no time for the game itself.
how_to_apply: Before taking a demanding lead role, decline or finish competing commitments. Focus on one directing job at a time. Before going independent, estimate how much of your time company management would eat. Keep a daily block that belongs only to your own tasks.
anti_pattern: Juggling other agreements while leading a project that needs everything; hiring staff by default and losing your creative time to running a company.
example: For Brawl, Sakurai turned down his other projects except Mushiking, which was already in progress (ep 132); Sora Ltd. stays a near-staffless contracting company so he can be a 'wandering director' (ep 53).
review_question: What else is competing for your attention on this project, and can you clear it?
keywords: focus commitment one project at a time overhead management independent studio freelancing time

principle: Picture the real people who will play, and let that fuel you
why: Imagining how people will react, and which parts they'll love, gives you the strength to push on. Real people will buy what you make, and what children love can shape their tastes for life. Imagining a presentation also organizes your thinking and can reveal new insights.
how_to_apply: While writing and developing, picture specific reactions to specific parts of the game. Mentally present your current build to customers and note what you would change. During hard stretches, share outside players' reactions with the team.
example: A child shouting 'Whoa! Look how far he flew!' at a Falcon Punch while playtesting the original Smash Bros. (ep 248); Smash Ultimate as the top game in a 2019 CoroCoro Comic survey (ep 124).
review_question: Which moment in this build do you picture players loving, and has anyone outside the team reacted to it yet?
keywords: motivation audience player reactions imagine presentation children morale purpose empathy

principle: Respect the labor behind every game, and judge it by its own goals
why: Every game has its own values, goals and audience, so ranking games on one scale misses what makes them great. Developers go through cuts and hardship to finish, and many games never ship at all. Creators who leave the industry often succeed elsewhere, and everyone has the right to choose their own path.
how_to_apply: Evaluate a game against what it set out to do for its intended players. Approach other developers' games with gratitude for the struggle behind them. Frame awards as celebration, not a race. Don't write off creators who disappear from view, and give yourself the same freedom to start something new.
anti_pattern: Choosing one universal 'best' game; treating sales as a measure of ingenuity; calling vanished creators washed up.
example: The Game Designers Award, judged on originality by directors of unique games (ep 13); master-up often leaving the team feeling wounded rather than triumphant (ep 87); Sakurai starting a YouTube channel while still making games (ep 176).
review_question: When you critique another game, are you judging it against its own goals and audience?
keywords: gratitude respect critique other developers awards judging empathy industry culture career change

principle: Study your genre's roots, then carve a new path
why: The path today's creators walk was carved by their predecessors. Playing the foundational games shows how clever ideas built on top of each other, and knowing that path is the basis for creating your own.
how_to_apply: Play landmark games of your genre and note which mechanic each introduced and what it cost. Then aim your own design at something those games didn't do instead of retracing them.
anti_pattern: Learning a genre only from its latest entries; retracing an old path instead of extending it.
example: Scramble's separate shot and bomb buttons and fuel gauge laid groundwork for side-scrollers like Gradius; Donkey Kong popularized jumping; Moon Patrol had possibly the first parallax scrolling (ep 155); 1986's jumps in storage capacity (ep 209).
review_question: Which classic first did what your core mechanic does, and what does yours add?
keywords: history classics arcade foundational games study roots retro conventions predecessors genre

principle: Don't let convenient tools or obvious answers fence in your ideas
why: If you're too tied to convenient systems, it's hard to step away from them and you set mental limits on what's possible; creation is about freedom. The obvious choice isn't always right, and proactively searching for new solutions tends to pay off.
how_to_apply: Regularly ask which 'impossible' ideas are only the limits of a tool or convention. Before adopting the standard solution (a stock rig, a raw leaderboard, a template site), consider at least one alternative built for your game.
anti_pattern: Treating a tool's defaults as the boundary of what's possible.
example: Realistic skeleton rigs limit joints to 180 degrees, while great animation pushes past common sense (ep 236); Smash's Global Smash Power instead of a standard leaderboard (ep 170).
review_question: Which limit in your design comes from a tool's default rather than from the game?
keywords: tools limits conventions creativity freedom thinking outside the box defaults constraints

principle: Use advice to sharpen your own judgment, not to replace it
why: Sakurai says the foundation is the viewer's own experience, skill and way of thinking; his lessons are only a boost, and mileage varies. Knowledge has meaning only when someone uses it.
how_to_apply: Test each lesson against your own build, keep what fits, and keep making and playing games to build the judgment the advice depends on.
anti_pattern: Following design rules blindly; collecting advice without applying any of it.
example: He calls the channel a 'boost' and closes the series with 'If nobody uses it, it might as well not exist!' (ep 1, 261).
review_question: Which piece of advice did you apply this week, and did it actually fit your game?
keywords: advice judgment learning experience rules of thumb apply knowledge mileage may vary
